STUTTGART 40 / GERMANY
PROF. DR. JEANNE HERSCH, UNIVERSITY OF GENEVA
Karl Jaspers and his Philosophy

It was by pure chance that I went to Heidelberg at the age of eighteen to learn German. It was my first term away from home. Since my main subject in Geneva had been Latin, I joined a Latin seminar in Heidelberg. We were reading Virgil’s Georgics and I can still remember our endless discussions on the following question: after a number of gods have been evoked by name at the beginning of the first Book, comes the passage “… and ye all, gods and goddesses;” our problem was to decide whether the expression “ye all” included the deities already mentioned, or whether it referred only to the others, i.e. those not yet named. While this discussion was going on, I used to count the clouds sailing across the sky as they passed the window of our classroom.

One day, as I was walking through our beautiful old refectory (formerly the castle stables), I met a girl who asked me whether I had heard Jaspers yet – she herself went to hear him from time to time. I said, “No, who is he?” She answered lightly, “I’d drop in there, if I were you – it’s interesting.”

I went. The lecture was in the old auditorium maximum. There, for the first time, I heard German as it is spoken in the North – with its clear, as it were transparent, s-p, s-t, sprechen, stehen. And there for the first time I saw that uplifted hand, that long hand, two fingers outstretched, two fingers folded back – which has always remained for me as a symbol that whatever is said in philosophy is not yet the last word.

At that time I had no more than the faintest glimmerings of philosophy. My German was very poor. I understood hardly anything of the lecture; but I did realize clearly that there was something here to be understood. I asked one of the students to give me a short summary of the lectures which I had missed in earlier weeks. By
chance he knew French and he was surprised to find that I was able to complete for him some of the sentences he had only just begun. “Have you read anything about these things before?,” he asked me.

A few days later, Jaspers’ lectures had become such an integral part of my life and happiness that I decided to try and join his Seminar as well. At that time he was reading Hegel’s Aesthetics with his students. They all told me it was terribly difficult and that they themselves could hardly keep pace with their reading from one session to the next. But I still wanted to make the attempt. It was no easy task to persuade someone to lend me the Hegel volume just for one night, so that I could judge for myself whether I could understand his language at all. I still remember how I would sit down under the lamp in my room and concentrate hard on the effort to read. It was certainly laborious. But after half an hour I was inclined to be optimistic: it’s hard (I thought), but it’s possible. But then, when I had closed the book and tried to remember what I had read, I realized in despair that nothing had registered. I tried again. This time I forced myself to write a summary (in French) of the content of every section. And in this way I continued to work into the small hours.

The next day, before the Seminar opened, I knocked at the door of the professor’s study. When the door opened, I had to look up and up till my eyes reached Jaspers’ head. And then I told him that I was French-speaking, understood very little, could not possibly write any essays for the Seminar or join in discussions, but would very much like to be allowed to attend the sessions as a silent listener. Jaspers advised against it – the term was too far advanced, I should benefit very little, it was not worth while. I took leave of him, apologized and turned to go. But then my disappointment must somehow have been apparent, for at the last moment Jaspers said: “But if you still wish to come, you may do so.” I did, and I stayed.

A third of a century has passed since then. I’m still there. I cannot even imagine what I should be if I had not encountered Jaspers’ philosophy. And the fact that we – his pupils and friends – are today permitted to celebrate his eightieth birthday floods us with infinite gratitude.

It is not only that we rejoice because of his presence in our midst over so long a period – so that, even when we do not see him or speak to him for a considerable time, we are still aware that somewhere that clear profound look of his still exists; that somewhere there is

steadfastness and faith; that somewhere the present era is being felt, understood, and experienced with passionate lucidity. It means more than this: the effect of his work on future generations will certainly be influenced by the fact that he has been able to defy the verdict of the doctors who, when he was twenty years old, told him he had no future; that he mastered so completely the art of living with his illness and was yet able to create one of the greatest and most important works of our time; that he lived through all the crises which shattered his own country, Europe, the world, and the whole epoch — by preserving in each new situation his unsullied clarity of vision and steadfastness of decision.

This would not be so important in the case of other philosophers. And I am not now referring to those whose lives one would prefer to forget because these are so little compatible with the style of their work and the aspirations expressed therein — whose genius appears to be the result so to speak of a sudden inspiration, a mercifully accorded gift, not a product of their own freedom — as if indeed some other person had been guiding the pen as they wrote. But even in the case of those thinkers whose signature is so much a part of their work that the work’s main function is to maintain their presence amongst us — even in these cases we may be confronted with the short-lived glow of a single flame, of an agonized outcry, a moment of ecstasy. This has the effect of fixing for all eternity (as in a mask) the most poignant moment of a tragic crisis or of a revelation — and then it is quite unimportant whether or not the author lives on.

The case of Karl Jaspers is very different. His philosophy, like that of a Socrates, a Spinoza, or a Kant, is derived, not from a single momentary experience, but from the efforts of a lifetime, and from the character of what emerges therefrom. Time, with its wearying repetitions which put everything to the test and threaten erosion, is a decisive factor in the moulding of quality; it is not the surprising, the unexpected that prevents style from banality, but faithfulness. Style, that monotony which speaks of being.

There is no other thinker in whom philosophy takes on such a superb — one might almost say such a sacred — meaning, while at the same time being anything but self-sufficient. For Jaspers, philosophy is of ultimate seriousness. Our whole being is bound by it. Indeed, it is itself our bond, and yet also the ever more clearly emerging consciousness that we derive from it and its absolute character. But it is also a bondage without a confession of faith, because one of the decisive steps in philosophic thought is the very proof that this is an

impossibility. Further: it is a bondage which excludes any blind submission to a factual, secular, or religious authority — even the authority of a book or the written word. To what then is one bound? That is the question put ironically by so many believers. Do we bind ourselves to reject every obligation and to preserve nothing but the tolerance that enables individuals and nations with differing ideals to exist side by side without violence — i. e. the agnosticism of the Enlightenment? That would merely mean preferring peace to truth, and even sacrificing truth to peace. But for Jaspers there can be no true peace that is not constantly nourished on a passion for truth.

Philosophical obligation is an “objectless” obligation, just because it denotes obligation to the truth. Truth — if that is what we are genuinely seeking, not some kind of substitute for it — is something that nobody can ever possess. This is not due to our lack of knowledge. On the contrary: the more we know, the longer grow the paths stretching into infinity which open up to us new, hitherto unknown, vistas. The reason lies in the nature of Truth itself. To us only objects are known; but Truth is not an object. Nor is it a subject. It is the horizon of Being into which every kind of established, acquired, and formulated knowledge is assimilated within that realm of Being that comprises a subject directed to an object. All objective knowledge leads towards and strives to attain this horizon of Truth. Only if we are suffering from a paralysis of our desire for the truth can we be satisfied with specialized or general knowledge whose meaning is restricted to a particular point of view and particular methods; only then could we mistake this for Truth itself.
Philosophical obligation has, therefore, no object, because Truth cannot be an object.

But although it has no object, it nevertheless involves a pledge — and this pledge is absolute. For Truth merges with Being. Philosophical commitment — because it cannot reach its appropriate object (since this “object” cannot be an object) — finds itself so to speak sentenced to a pledge which is being. Not the Being that transcends the division into subject and object — in which the commitment dimly divines its own ultimate origin —, but the Being of the individual committed, who binds himself to exist. What does this mean? For the individual who, bound by philosophical obligation, dedicates himself to fulfil — within his concrete, particular, and limited sphere of action — all the possibilities open to his nature, existence means

utilizing opportunities for acquiring knowledge and understanding, for making himself understood; occasions for decision and action; opportunities for love and struggle; possibilities of work, of creative activity; occasions for worship; and every opening for liberty which provides any hope of possible existence.

And thus we perceive that philosophy cannot be satisfied with itself alone. On the contrary, it demands as inescapable for its own genuineness that the philosophical individual prove his worth by search and understanding in the realm of knowledge, by active participation and assumption of responsibility in public life, by reliability in his attachments to the human beings closest to him, by seeking existential understanding between himself and the adherents of an exclusive religious faith.

It is therefore by no means sufficient to renounce any kind of dogmatism and merely worship the wisdom of the eternally closed Hand of God which conceals the truth from us. No. Through our acts we must answer that Being which in its withdrawal somehow speaks to us, and, replacing unattainable knowledge, become conscious in our freedom of the reality of that derivative finite Being with which we have been endowed.

As Jaspers conceives it, philosophy is thus not a science. And if science should claim either to be able to solve the problems of philosophy, or authoritatively to reject it as being of no importance, it would be untrue to its own strict principles. Nevertheless, Jaspers himself looks on the pursuit of science not only as a necessary activity in itself, but also as one of the indispensable conditions for existence and for genuine philosophical thought. On the negative side it is science itself that, under the strict conditions of its general validity, allows the relativity and limitations of the scope of its findings to be clearly perceptible. On the positive side, philosophy finds in science the language — which changes in every era — which it needs in order to speak indirectly of transcendent Being. But there is more to it than this: by means of its general and empirical validity science, so to speak, maintains a standard of compelling insight which pursues existence even into those regions where it cannot be reached, where — instead — the uniqueness of existential obligation is realized. The absolutism of this obligation should itself be as clear as possible, and here again compulsive scientific insight acts as an unattainable but indispensable ideal which never ceases to demand complete clarity.

Jaspers' enthusiasm for scientific research — it should always be borne in mind that he studied medicine, practised as a doctor, and worked for many years in laboratories — is strenuously opposed to the comprehensive contemporary syntheses that are so widely applauded by the public today. Those syntheses attempt to set up a continuous objective unity in which all the different aspects of the world as well as of human history find a place; they even venture to promise "by tomorrow" the total and supreme convergence of knowledge and human worship. Jaspers' conception is entirely different. No thinker resists the temptations presented by a given synthesis or an inescapable eschatology more energetically. On the contrary: the greater the progress achieved by the sciences, the more clearly perceptible become the heterogeneous nature of their methods and points of view — and in consequence their discontinuity and essential plurality.

Discontinuity and plurality are for Existence signs of the impossibility of a scientifically complete world-image — a world in which Liberty would suffocate, because in it Existence would be like some object contained in a larger object and thus submitted to the constitutive laws of objectivity. In Jaspers' conception the words "Unity" and "Totality" regain their true function — the Kantian function of ideas: regulatory and not constitutive, set as tasks, not as given rules. And therewith Being is for ever denied the inertia and irresponsibility which any universal synthesis, however dynamically interpreted, would entail by means of its objective order or progress. What the world is, what the world will become, still depends on such liberty as may be realized in it.

The less human decisions are supported by some impersonal, deductive, or technical necessity of a scientific nature, the clearer becomes the absolutely obligatory nature in every concrete situation confronting the person who makes the decision. Will, Choice, Faith — these are, as it were, oaths sworn by Existence to Transcendence, and thus like metaphysical ciphers of Being; for Being, as sole root of everything unconditioned, has alone made them possible.

And so, in Jaspers' conception, free actions are in the highest state of tension between (on the one hand) Transcendence to which they owe the absoluteness of their decision and, on the other, the concrete circumstances in which these actions are historically developed. No conceptual or technical bridge can span these two planes.

On the plane of concrete circumstances the free act demands the utmost clarity, as well as knowledge and critical judgment of facts and information; the use of all available methods to enlarge one's outlook; and the capability of estimating causes and possible or probable consequences in order that the true possibilities may be seen in their proper light. The same bond that links Existence to Transcendence demands that the historical environment of any decision be interpreted in the harshest possible light. And hence comes Jaspers' rejection of any obscurity; of any monopoly of knowledge as the privilege of a few great initiates whom the general public have only to believe and to trust; and of any propaganda or untruths, however kindly meant and compassionate they might be. And hence also Jaspers' opposition to any somersaults by which reason would renounce its rights and duties.

But, however rigorously clarified, the absolute demand does not in itself promise success. The best decision does not necessarily emerge from painstaking and conscientious probing. And so it remains tied to Transcendence and from that it receives its absolute weight of existential responsibility.

That is why the confrontation of Existence with Existence is of quite a different kind from that of scholars with each other. True, Existence uses the language of reason when conferring with the other Existence; for it is the only common language available to mankind. But here this language does not develop a system of arguments designed to force an impersonal unmistakable truth on all participants. On this plane an apparently rational victory would not necessarily mean a victory of Truth. Here it is not a question of objective but of existential truth — and existential truth can never be independent of the language in which it is expressed, or of the mouth which expresses it. It is not even independent of what happens among the participants in the course of confrontation, or of what each participant is thinking or feeling; and the words that are used may be transformed by their own effectiveness. Thus the confrontation becomes a kind of existential exercise in which Existence makes sure of itself, and of the kind of Truth it aims to attain.

But when we are considering the kind of Truth that is not to be forced on anybody as a fixed result, but which is realized in the course of the confrontation itself, then any defeat of one individual would paralyse the existential search of the other and destroy the conditions of Truth. The presence of an opponent, his liberty,

his unconditioned state are as necessary to me as my own. The struggle between us does not permit of the polite modulations of social conversation. The struggle, as Jaspers says, is radical and ruthless. But — because of this very fact, not despite of it, it is a loving conflict; for what I want is not victory, not destruction of my opponent, but both for him and for myself that truth that neither he nor I can capture in rational apodictic language.

We are not concerned with winning the argument. Our concern is never to forsake the use of reason in order to reach the richer possibilities of what lies beyond any reason. Jaspers has shown over and over again how Transcendence escapes from Reason — by caging it in the superficial enclosures of circles, contradictions, and tautologies — thus manifesting itself to us.

The liberty must not be stifled or diminished by any kind of institution — neither a political nor a religious institution. On the contrary: the only justification for any institution lies in the possibilities it secures for this liberty. This is the standard that Jaspers consistently sets for his political views — the profound, the absolute root of his opposition to any kind of attempted totalitarianism. And if there is nothing of the anarchist in his make-up — if he lays great stress on the necessity for Authority — that is because he defends metaphysical liberty, not in the realm of words or literature, but in that of specific decisions in a given historical situation and here his studies and experience have taught him that in human societies Freedom without Authority entails the self-destruction of Freedom.

In his anxiety for the preservation of Liberty Jaspers, shortly before Hitler seized power, published a serious warning: he had realized that an empty, insubstantial, abstract Freedom would not be able to withstand any attack by violence, any temptation to cowardly abdication. After the years of silence and ganger under Hitler's rule, immediately after Germany's defeat, Jaspers gave his lecture on the Guilt Question. In the midst of the ruins of the German Reich and of the cities, he strode straight forward to the most urgent of all tasks, i. e. to obtain a clear view, unobscured by partiality or by masochism, of what had been done, in order to pave the way for the resurgence of true Liberty. There could hardly be a more impressive view of the nature of the relations between the existential urge towards Transcendence and the relentless search for clarity. An urge which excludes any obscurity, every untruth, every political or ethical strategy, in order to let nothing prevail except that which is true. From the same point of

view of Liberty Jaspers has in recent years — with great courage against the trend of public opinion — placed the national aim of re-uniting divided Germany below the far weightier concern for the freedom of man. The national State as such is unimportant. What counts is a true tradition of liberty for the individual human being. In Jaspers' work nobody will ever find a programme of political strategy or indeed any kind of political programme. Anything that might appear to be of this nature will only be a means of making clear what ought to be the basic meaning and fundamental norm of any policy, any strategy — namely the absolute value of the possibilities of liberty. Some people in Germany have believed that with these opinions Jaspers had disowned his Fatherland. But the contrary is the case; there could be no greater loyalty than his towards a certain kind of Germany — of which he seemed to find some trace in the small town of Basel in Switzerland — that is, a diversified Germany with small, limited political units, a Germany that knew how to value her diversity, her local and ordinary attachments, as the most fruitful soil for human freedom and its possibilities. Always the courageous figther against the stream, always despising the lying sentimentality of the knights of "eternal peace", Jaspers refused to appeal for unilateral abolition of atomic weapons, for peace at any price. On the contrary — he did not, as his opponents claimed, speak in favour of the bomb, but he championed a true peace, one that can only be of a supra-national nature. And he spoke for the Freedom that refuses to yield itself up here and now for fear of a future apocalypse, and which today as ever before claims the right to make its own decisions according to the situation at any particular moment.

And that is not the only way in which Jaspers has applied his philosophy to the actual happenings of daily life. He has lived among the great philosophers of the past, understanding them, interpreting them, making them his own — as with his existential friends — lived with them in reverence and in discussion, and has generously allowed us all to share them with him. He has been a lifelong friend of those still alive. And finally his loyalties reach their peak in his marriage. Today, as ever, his wife is by his side, devoted to him and yet, as ever, totally herself. Wer are experiencing a great, a beautiful and a happy day.

Many people, even today, do not really know what they want. Propaganda, working through self-interest and force without regard for truth or fiction, takes possession of the mind which does not think for itself and so offers but weak resistance. It is inevitable that truth today must take on the form of propaganda in order to reach men's ears. It is thus the great task of creative thinking to lay stress on the simple, fundamental truths, in order that they may echo in the intellect, with which all men are endowed.

In opposing the claim to absolute knowledge, philosophy has the task of keeping alive individual thought, and through it the personality of the individual which would be extinguished under totalitarian regimes. It must, indeed, remind every individual that he may find and develop his own personality, and that he ceases to be human, if he renounces this possibility. For the sake of our common future it is imperative that we should transform thought into action with enlightened motives and with the deepest sense of responsibility.
